prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

SRINAGAR, Indian-controlled Kashmir (CNN) -- Anti-election demonstrators threw stones at two polling stations and clashed with Indian security forces Sunday as voters stood in long lines in Indian-controlled Kashmir to cast ballots in the second stage of state elections. An Indian Border Security Forces soldier watches as voters in Indian-controlled Kashmir wait to vote Sunday. The protesters yelled pro-independence and anti-poll slogans and threw stones at polling stations in two villages in the Ganderbal constituency, police said. Police used batons to restore order, but no one was injured, police said. People demonstrated in two other villages, Duderhama and Beehama in Ganderbal constituency -- one of six constituencies voting Sunday in the second of seven stages in the state assembly elections. The elections began after months of violent protests by anti-Indian groups, fearful state elections will firm up Indian control of the Muslim majority Himalayan state, and by Indian nationalists, fearful that separatist groups will gain control. Kashmir, divided between India and Pakistan and claimed by both, has been wracked by an 18-year bloody separatist campaign that authorities say has left at least 43,000 dead. Sunday's protests came a day after Indian paramilitary forces, according to authorities, gunned down two youths, one of them a high school student apparently taking part in an anti-India demonstration. Police Saturday fired on protesters in the town of Baramulla, killing 10th-grader Manzoor Ahmad Kumar, a senior police officer told CNN. Hundreds of protesters followed Kumar's body into the "Old Town" area of Baramulla, where demonstrators clashed with police. Protesters threw stones at a candidate's escort vehicles, the office said. Indian authorities deployed heavy paramilitary and police reinforcements to maintain order. Six protesters were injured in the fighting, police said. A police official said paramilitary forces in the Baramulla's Old Town area Saturday, shot and killed a second youth, Tanvir Ahmad Sheikh. Elsewhere Sunday, voting continued without incident. In Kangan constituency, voting picked up in the late morning and afternoon, and there and in Ganderbal, voters -- including many women -- lined up to cast their votes. Indian poll officials said the turnout was about 65 percent of eligible voters. Heavy security was also deployed in Srinagar, the summer capital of Indian-administered Kashmir. Indian paramilitary troopers carried automatic weapons and blocked roads with barricades and coils of razor wire there and in other towns.   The first phase of elections was held November 17 and the third will be held November 30.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about clashes between anti-election protesters and Indian security forces during the second phase of state elections in Indian-controlled Kashmir, including details on voter turnout, polling stations, recent deaths in Baramulla, and the broader Kashmir conflict.
counterfactuals.output:
**Srinagar, Indian-controlled Kashmir (CNN)** — Anti-election protesters clashed with Indian security forces Tuesday as voters cast ballots in the second phase of state assembly elections in Indian-controlled Kashmir, a region long at the center of a bitter dispute between India and Pakistan.

The voting took place under heavy security across 18 constituencies, with thousands of police and paramilitary troops deployed around polling stations. Election officials said turnout was about **71%**, a high figure in a region where separatist groups have repeatedly called for election boycotts. More than **2,000 polling stations** were set up for the phase, serving voters across parts of the Kashmir Valley as well as Jammu and Ladakh regions.

In several areas, including parts of Baramulla district, groups of young protesters threw stones at security forces and shouted anti-India and pro-freedom slogans, witnesses said. Security personnel responded with tear gas and baton charges to disperse crowds near polling areas. There were no immediate official reports of major injuries during the clashes.

The unrest came amid heightened tensions following recent deaths in **Baramulla**, where local anger has grown after security operations and militant-related violence in the district. The deaths have fueled calls by separatist leaders for protests and a boycott of the election, which they describe as illegitimate under Indian rule.

Indian authorities have portrayed the strong turnout as evidence of public faith in the democratic process, while separatist groups argue that voting under a large security presence does not reflect the region’s political aspirations.

Kashmir has been divided between India and Pakistan since 1947, and both countries claim the territory in full. Indian-controlled Kashmir has witnessed an armed insurgency since 1989, with militant groups seeking either independence or a merger with Pakistan. Tens of thousands of people — civilians, militants and security personnel — have been killed in the conflict.

India accuses Pakistan of supporting militant groups operating in Kashmir, a charge Islamabad denies, saying it provides only diplomatic and moral support to Kashmiris seeking self-determination.

The multi-phase state election is being held amid tight security and calls for boycott from separatist leaders. Despite periodic violence, election officials said polling continued through the day, with long lines reported in several rural areas.

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a wire-service style report about voting in Indian-administered Kashmir amid separatist protests, with background on the India-Pakistan dispute, casualties from the insurgency, and the schedule of the seven-stage election.
counterfactuals.output:
SRINAGAR, Indian-administered Kashmir — Voters cast ballots under tight security Monday in the opening stage of a seven-phase election in Indian-administered Kashmir, as separatist groups staged protests and called for a boycott of the polls.

Thousands of police and paramilitary troops were deployed around polling stations across the Himalayan region, where separatist leaders have denounced the election as illegitimate and urged residents to stay away. Authorities restricted movement in some areas and detained or closely monitored prominent separatist figures ahead of the vote.

The election is being held in seven stages because of security concerns and the region’s difficult terrain. Polling is scheduled for Nov. 17, Nov. 23, Nov. 30, Dec. 7, Dec. 13, Dec. 17 and Dec. 24, with counting due on Dec. 28.

India says the vote is a democratic exercise to choose a state government to handle local issues. Separatists argue that elections cannot substitute for a political settlement over Kashmir’s status. Many separatist groups either seek independence or merger with Pakistan.

Kashmir has been at the center of a dispute between India and Pakistan since the two countries won independence from Britain in 1947. Both claim the territory in full but govern it in parts. The rivals have fought two of their three wars over Kashmir, and the region remains one of the world’s most heavily militarized areas.

An armed insurgency against Indian rule erupted in 1989. Indian officials say tens of thousands of people have been killed in the violence, while rights groups and separatist organizations put the toll higher. Estimates commonly range from more than 47,000 dead according to official figures to about 70,000 or more cited by separatist and human rights groups.

The latest election follows months of unrest in the Kashmir Valley, where mass demonstrations and strikes have challenged Indian authority. Separatist leaders say participation in the vote would weaken their demand for self-determination, while mainstream political parties are campaigning on issues including jobs, roads, electricity and governance.

Despite boycott calls, past elections in the region have often produced mixed turnout, with higher participation in some rural and frontier districts and lower voting in separatist strongholds such as parts of Srinagar and other urban centers. Security officials said they were prepared for attempts to disrupt polling, while election authorities said arrangements had been made to allow voting to proceed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.output:
**Indian-controlled Kashmir votes in second stage of elections amid clashes and deadly unrest**

*CNN-style news report — original draft*

**Srinagar, Indian-controlled Kashmir** — Voters in Indian-controlled Kashmir cast ballots in the second stage of regional elections amid heightened security, scattered clashes at polling stations and fresh anger over the reported killings of two young men following an anti-India protest.

Election officials reported turnout of about **65 percent** in the latest phase of voting, a figure authorities described as a sign of public participation despite calls by separatist groups to boycott the polls.

But the day was marked by tension in several areas. Witnesses and local officials reported clashes near polling stations, where groups opposed to the election confronted security forces and, in some cases, attempted to disrupt voting. Police and paramilitary personnel were deployed in large numbers across the region, with checkpoints set up on major roads and near voting centers.

In **Baramulla**, in northern Kashmir, tensions escalated after an anti-India protest. Two youths were killed in the aftermath, according to local reports, triggering outrage among residents and renewed demonstrations. The circumstances of the killings remained disputed, with locals accusing security forces of using excessive force, while authorities said they were investigating the incident.

Kashmir, claimed by both India and Pakistan, has been one of the world’s most militarized regions for decades. Many Kashmiris oppose Indian rule, and elections in the region are often held under heavy security and shadowed by separatist boycott campaigns.

Indian officials have frequently pointed to voter turnout as evidence of confidence in the democratic process. Separatist leaders, however, argue that participation in local elections does not reflect acceptance of Indian sovereignty, saying many voters cast ballots to address local concerns such as roads, jobs, electricity and basic services.

The latest phase of voting is part of a multi-stage election process designed to allow security forces to be deployed across different districts. Authorities said polling was largely peaceful overall, despite the reported clashes and unrest.

The deaths in Baramulla are likely to intensify criticism of the security response and could inflame tensions as the remaining stages of voting continue.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a detailed news story from Srinagar about Kashmir’s state assembly elections proceeding under tight security despite anti-election protests, including incidents in Ganderbal, Baramulla, Kangan, and Srinagar.
counterfactuals.output:
**Srinagar:** Kashmir’s state assembly elections went ahead under an extensive security blanket on polling day, even as anti-election protests and sporadic clashes were reported from several parts of the Valley, including Ganderbal, Baramulla, Kangan and Srinagar.

From early morning, thousands of police, paramilitary and security personnel were deployed across sensitive areas, guarding polling stations, roads and government buildings. Checkpoints were set up at key intersections, vehicles were stopped and searched, and patrols moved through neighborhoods where separatist groups had called for a boycott of the vote.

Despite the tense atmosphere, election officials said polling began as scheduled at most stations. Voters were seen lining up outside some booths, particularly in areas where security forces had sealed off approach roads. In other pockets, polling remained thin as residents stayed indoors, either in response to boycott calls or out of fear of violence.

The day was marked by anti-election demonstrations in several areas. In **Ganderbal**, groups of protesters took to the streets shouting slogans against the election process. Security forces intervened to disperse the crowds, leading to brief clashes. Witnesses said stones were thrown at security personnel, who responded with baton charges and tear smoke shells in some localities. Polling staff were reportedly moved under escort in areas considered vulnerable.

In **Baramulla**, one of the Valley’s more volatile districts during periods of unrest, protesters attempted to block roads leading to polling stations. Security forces quickly moved in to clear the routes. Local residents reported a heavy presence of police and paramilitary personnel throughout the town and nearby villages. Officials said voting was not halted, though turnout varied sharply from one neighborhood to another.

Tension was also reported in **Kangan**, where demonstrators gathered near polling areas and raised slogans calling for a boycott. Security personnel prevented the protesters from marching toward election facilities. The confrontation led to stone-pelting in some spots, prompting security forces to use crowd-control measures. Authorities said additional reinforcements were sent to the area to ensure voting continued.

In **Srinagar**, the summer capital and the political center of the region, security was especially tight. Barricades were placed on major roads, and personnel in riot gear were posted outside polling stations, government offices and sensitive neighborhoods. Anti-election protesters tried to assemble in parts of the city, but police dispersed them before they could gather in large numbers. Shops in some areas remained closed, while traffic was sparse during the morning hours.

Election officials maintained that the polling process remained largely on track despite the disturbances. “There were isolated incidents of protest and stone-pelting, but voting continued under security arrangements,” an official said. Polling staff, electronic voting machines and other election materials had been transported to stations under heavy escort, with contingency plans in place for flashpoints.

Security officials said the heightened deployment was necessary because militant groups and separatist organizations had urged people to stay away from the polls. Authorities had warned that attempts could be made to disrupt the process through protests, intimidation or attacks on election-related infrastructure.

The elections are being closely watched as a test of political participation in a region long marked by conflict, separatist sentiment and deep distrust of government institutions. While mainstream political parties have urged voters to use the ballot to address local grievances, anti-election groups have described the exercise as illegitimate and called for a complete boycott.

For many voters, the decision to participate was driven by local concerns rather than broader political questions. Some who turned out said they wanted better roads, jobs, electricity and public services. Others said they stayed away because of the boycott call or because they believed voting would not change the political situation.

By late afternoon, security forces remained deployed in strength across the Valley, particularly in areas where protests had been reported. Officials said they were monitoring the situation closely and would maintain heightened security until polling teams and election materials were safely returned to collection centers.

While the day saw no major breakdown of the election process, the protests in Ganderbal, Baramulla, Kangan and Srinagar underscored the continuing tensions surrounding elections in Kashmir, where every vote is held under the shadow of conflict, security restrictions and competing political narratives.
